variplex does two things for engineers who work with variability models:

  1. It builds the graphs. For a variability model, variplex computes every relationship between two features that holds in all its valid configurations:

    • requires: every valid configuration with A also has B;
    • excludes: no valid configuration has both A and B;
    • at least one: no valid configuration lacks both.

    The model can be a feature model in UVL, or the Boolean formula (DIMACS) of a model written in any other notation, such as the Kconfig files of the Linux kernel translated by KMax, KConfigReader or KconfigSampler. The graphs are synthesized once using a SAT solver and an auxiliary graph called Modal Implication Graph (MIG).

  2. It analyses the graphs. More than a hundred functions answer questions about them without calling a solver again, and return tibbles: what each feature weighs, how the model is layered, where its conflicts come from, which features can go together, how much of the model a test sample covers, which patterns recur, and how the model changes from version to version.

Installation 

install.packages("variplex")

Nothing has to be installed outside R. To draw the graphs, install also the suggested packages DiagrammeR (and DiagrammeRsvg and rsvg to save drawings as SVG, PDF or PNG). The development version is on GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("rheradio/variplex")

Example 

library(variplex)

band <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"), or_graph = TRUE)
band
#> variplex model "miband3_realized"
#>   features: 11 variable (the nodes of the graphs), 8 core, 0 dead
#>   requires: 21 arrows   excludes: 10 lines
#>   at least one: 3 lines
#>   atomic sets: 1 (of two or more features)

vp_requirements(band, "TouchScreen") # what the touch screen brings along
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>   feature       
#>   <chr>         
#> 1 Screen        
#> 2 OLED          
#> 3 CapacityButton
# why two features never go together
vp_explain_conflict(band, "MovementFilter", "BT40")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>   origin  step from           link     to    
#>    <int> <int> <chr>          <chr>    <chr> 
#> 1      1     1 MovementFilter requires BLEv40
#> 2      1     2 BLEv40         requires Screen
#> 3      1     3 Screen         excludes BT40
vp_can_go_together(
  band,
  list(c("TouchScreen", "HeartRateSensor"), c("TouchScreen", "BT40"))
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   wish                         possible reasons                                          
#>   <chr>                        <lgl>    <chr>                                            
#> 1 TouchScreen, HeartRateSensor TRUE     ""                                               
#> 2 TouchScreen, BT40            FALSE    "TouchScreen (which brings Screen) excludes BT40"
vp_plot(vp_minimal(band))                          # with DiagrammeR

Documentation

Start with vignette("variplex"). The other vignettes go through the results (vignette("graphs")) and every question the graphs answer, topic by topic; vp_functions() lists the functions by topic.

What the graphs cannot see

The graphs hold relationships between two features. A rule that ties three or more features at once (“A requires B or C”) is in no graph, unless it implies a relationship between two of them. Everything the graphs say is true; a “yes” to a long wish list can still be wrong. vignette("limits-theory") explains it, measures it and proves it.

Citation

citation("variplex"). The dataset of graphs of 5,709 variability models is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17277788.
